title: Books and Words
description: Ten stories and short texts about a used-book store, a translator, word histories, a poetry night, a book launch, a bookmobile and other places where books and words matter.

lessons.title: The Store on Willow Street
lessons.summary: Ruth's small used-book store is full of narrow rooms, fresh coffee and a very lazy cat.
lessons.text:
At the end of Willow Street, under an old willow tree, there is a small store that sells used books. Its owner, Ruth Palmer, opened it 30 years ago and named it after the tree: The Willow. In summer, the long branches of the willow hang low over the door, so that customers have to push them aside to come in.

Inside, the store is a warren of narrow rooms, where one room leads to another. New visitors often get lost in this warren, but nobody minds. In the main room, the books rise from the floor to the ceiling, and the ceiling is so high that Ruth has to stand on a chair to reach the top. In the back rooms, the ceiling is low, and tall customers quickly learn to bend their heads.

The floor is covered with an old red carpet. Near the door, the carpet has worn thin, because thousands of feet have crossed it over the years. Ruth refuses to replace it. "This carpet has met every customer I have ever had," she likes to say.

Every morning at eight, Ruth grinds coffee in a small machine behind the counter. The noise of the grinding fills the quiet rooms, and soon a rich, warm smell follows. She offers a cup to anyone who stays longer than ten minutes. Some customers say the coffee has the flavor of chocolate; others say its flavor reminds them of fresh bread.

Near the front window, a cluster of old soft chairs stands around a low table. On wet afternoons, the cluster is full of readers: students with their school books, a young mother with a sleeping baby, and an old man who reads history books every Saturday.

The store also has a cat, an enormous orange cat called Oscar. He is so enormous that small children think he is a dog, and he is probably the laziest cat in the city. Oscar does not catch mice, and he does not greet anyone. He spends the whole day asleep in a nest of old newspapers in the poetry section. Ruth has tried to move his nest twice, but each time, Oscar built a new nest in exactly the same place. Lazy as he is, the customers love him, and some children come in only to see him.

The Willow is not a large store, and it will never make Ruth rich. Still, for the people of Willow Street, it is like a second living room.

Questions:
Why is the store called The Willow?
Ruth named it after the old willow tree that grows in front of it.
Why do new visitors often get lost?
They get lost because the store is a warren of narrow rooms.
Why does Ruth refuse to replace the old red carpet?
She says that the carpet has met every customer she has ever had.
What does Ruth do every morning at eight?
She grinds coffee in a small machine behind the counter.
Who sits in the cluster of chairs on wet afternoons?
Students, a young mother with her baby and an old man who reads history books sit there.
Where does Oscar sleep?
The lazy cat sleeps in a nest of old newspapers in the poetry section.

lessons.title: A Translator's Day
lessons.summary: Elena, who translates Spanish novels into English, describes an ordinary working day.
lessons.text:
My name is Elena Ruiz, and I translate novels from Spanish into English. People often imagine that my job is exciting. Let me describe an ordinary Tuesday, so that you can judge for yourself.

At seven, I sit down at my desk and boot up my old computer. It takes almost five minutes to boot, so I usually read the news while I wait. Once the computer has booted, I open the book I am working on, a long family story set in a small village in Spain.

My day follows a simple pattern: I alternate between translating and revising. In the morning, when my mind is fresh, I translate new pages. In the afternoon, I revise the pages I wrote the day before. I alternate like this because a tired mind cannot create much, but it can still find mistakes. I often revise a single page four or five times.

Many people have the notion that translation is a simple equation: one Spanish word equals one English word, and you only have to solve the equation. That notion is completely wrong. Words carry feelings and history, not just meanings. The grandmother in this novel, for example, speaks with a strong country accent, and her accent tells the reader where she grew up and how she sees the world. I cannot copy a Spanish accent in English, so I adjust her sentences instead. I make them shorter, a little old-fashioned and full of country images. If I adjust too much, she sounds like a different woman.

A translator must also stay neutral. Even if I do not like a character, I must not make him sound worse than the author did. My job is to be a clean window, not a colored one, and a neutral window lets the reader see the story as it is.

At twelve, I have a video call with the author, Mateo Vargas. Our respect is mutual: he trusts my English, and I trust his story. We also have a mutual friend, a poet in Madrid who introduced us five years ago. He always begins formally. "Dear Elena, regarding the word on page 112, I believe the meaning is closer to 'sad' than to 'tired.'" Then he laughs and adds, "But honestly? Just make it sound good."

My publisher in Madrid pays me about 20 euros for each finished page. I will never become rich, but 20 euros a page pays the rent.

At six, I turn off the computer and go for a long walk. Tomorrow I will alternate again.

Questions:
What does Elena do while her computer boots?
She reads the news while she waits.
How does Elena alternate her work?
She translates new pages in the morning and revises old pages in the afternoon.
Why is translation not a simple equation?
Words carry feelings and history, not just meanings, so one word does not simply equal another.
How does Elena show the grandmother's country accent in English?
She adjusts the grandmother's sentences and makes them shorter and a little old-fashioned.
Why must a translator stay neutral?
A translator must not make a character sound better or worse than the author did.
How much does Elena earn for each page?
She earns about 20 euros for each finished page.

lessons.title: Where Words Come From
lessons.summary: A short column on the long journeys of a few ordinary English words.
lessons.text:
Every word has a history. We use words every day without thinking about them, yet many of them traveled for centuries before they reached us.

Let us begin at the very beginning, with the letters themselves. The Greek alphabet starts with alpha and beta, and the English word "alphabet" is simply these two names joined together. Because alpha was the first letter, software companies still call the earliest test version of a new program the alpha version.

Many English words arrived with an army. In 1066, soldiers from Normandy crossed the sea and took over England. After the invasion, the new masters of the country spoke French, and for about 300 years French was the language of the court, the law and the rich. The invasion explains a curious detail. The animal in the field kept its old English name, cow, because the farmers who cared for it spoke English. The meat on rich tables, however, received a French name: beef.

The army also gave us the word sergeant. It comes from an old French word for a servant, and a sergeant was once simply a man who served a knight. Today, a sergeant gives orders rather than taking them.

Many family names began as occupations. A family called Baker probably had a baker in it long ago, someone who made the bread for a whole village. In the same way, the name Smith comes from a man who worked with metal. For centuries, a person's occupation was a large part of who they were, so the occupation became the name.

Words also travel with goods. Tobacco came to Europe from the Caribbean, and the word tobacco probably comes from the language of the Taino people who lived there. The burger arrived more recently. Its full name, hamburger, comes from the German city of Hamburg. People in the United States later made the name shorter, and today you can order a fish burger or even a vegetable burger.

Some words come from the classical languages, Latin and ancient Greek. In Roman times, a villa was a large house on a farm, where a rich family spent the hot summer. Today, a villa is usually an expensive house near the sea. Classical Latin also gave English many words for science.

Finally, some words arrived quite recently. Entrepreneur came from French about 200 years ago, from a verb that means "to take on" a task. An entrepreneur is a person who takes on the risk of starting a business.

So the next time you order a burger, remember that even a simple meal carries some history.

Questions:
Where does the word "alphabet" come from?
It comes from alpha and beta, the first two letters of the Greek alphabet.
What happened in 1066?
Soldiers from Normandy crossed the sea and took over England.
Why does the meat of a cow have a French name?
After the invasion, the rich people who ate the meat spoke French.
What did a sergeant once do?
A sergeant was once a man who served a knight.
Where does the word burger come from?
It comes from hamburger, a name taken from the German city of Hamburg.
What is an entrepreneur?
An entrepreneur is a person who takes on the risk of starting a business.

lessons.title: Poetry Night
lessons.summary: Maya reads her poem about a summer storm at the seventh grade's poetry night, with her friend dancing beside her.
lessons.text:
Every spring, the seventh grade at Lincoln Middle School holds a poetry night. Each seventh-grade student writes a poem and reads it out loud in the school hall, in front of parents, teachers and friends. Mr. Grant, who teaches English, calls it "the oral part" of the poetry lessons. "Poetry began as an oral art," he tells his class every year. "People spoke poems out loud long before anyone wrote them down."

This year, Maya Brooks was more nervous than anyone. Her poem was about a summer storm that she had watched from her grandmother's window: the dark clouds, the sudden wind, and a single bright arc of lightning over the fields. She had worked on it for three weeks. On paper, she liked it. Saying it out loud in front of a hundred people was another matter.

Her friend Jada, the best dancer in the class, offered to help. "What if I dance while you read?" she asked. "Then people will look at me, not at you." Maya laughed, but she agreed. Each poet could be accompanied by one friend, and Maya was happy to be accompanied by a dancer.

On poetry night, the hall was full. Some poems were funny, and some were sad. A quiet boy named Owen read a short poem about a bud on a cherry tree that waits all winter to open. He described the bud so carefully that, when he finished, the room was silent for a moment before everyone clapped. Earlier, Mr. Grant had reminded the audience that it is rude to talk or to check a phone while someone is reading, and nobody was rude that night.

Then it was Maya's turn. Her hands were shaking, but she began to read. Jada moved slowly at first, like the wind before a storm. When Maya reached the line about the lightning, Jada jumped and drew a sharp arc in the air with her arm, as quick as lightning itself. A stir went through the audience, and people leaned forward in their seats. By the end, Maya was no longer reading to the floor; she was looking straight at her parents.

Afterward, Mr. Grant shook Maya's hand. "Your poem showed real imagination," he said. "And tonight you used your imagination twice: once in the writing, and once in the reading." At the table with the cake and the hot chocolate, Maya's mother stirred her cup and could not stop smiling.

Questions:
What does each seventh-grade student do at the poetry night?
Each student writes a poem and reads it out loud in the school hall.
Why does Mr. Grant call poetry an oral art?
He says people spoke poems out loud long before anyone wrote them down.
What was Maya's poem about?
It was about a summer storm, with dark clouds, a sudden wind and an arc of lightning.
Who accompanied Maya, and what did she do?
Her friend Jada, a dancer, accompanied her and danced while Maya read.
What was Owen's poem about?
It was about a bud on a cherry tree that waits all winter to open.
What did Mr. Grant say about Maya's poem?
He said that it showed real imagination.

lessons.title: The First Book Launch
lessons.summary: Daniel is nervous about the launch of his first novel, but the evening goes better than he expected.
lessons.text:
Daniel Ortiz had wanted to write a book since he was ten years old. At 42, he finally held one in his hands: a novel about a fishing family on the coast of Maine. The launch was planned for a Thursday evening at a small bookstore downtown, and for two weeks Daniel could hardly sleep.

His sister Rosa had a name for his condition. "You have first book syndrome," she told him on the phone. "Every new writer has it. You think nobody will come, and if somebody comes, you think they will hate the book." Daniel had to admit that she had described the syndrome perfectly.

His own prediction was that five people would come, and that three of them would be family. Rosa's prediction was more positive: she said at least 40. "Your predictions are always too dark," she said. "Mine are usually right."

The plan for the evening was conventional. Daniel would read for twenty minutes, answer questions and then sign books. The owner of the store, a calm woman called Mrs. Alvarez, told him that a conventional launch is the best kind. "People like to know what will happen," she said. "Read slowly, and smile."

The night before the launch, Daniel made a pledge to himself. For years, he had avoided speaking in public, but now he pledged that he would confront his fear instead of running from it. He would confront it in front of strangers.

On the evening of the launch, he arrived ten minutes late because of the traffic, so his first words were an apology. "I'm very sorry," he said. "That is my first and last apology tonight." People laughed, and something in the room relaxed.

A considerable crowd had come: about 60 people, including old friends from school, two of his teachers and many strangers who had read about the book in the local newspaper. It was a considerable surprise to Daniel, but not to Rosa, who sat in the front row looking pleased with herself.

As Daniel read, his fear slowly disappeared. By the third page, his voice was steady, and he even looked up from the book now and then. The questions were kind and intelligent. By the end of the evening, all the books on the table had disappeared as well, because Mrs. Alvarez had sold every copy.

Later, Rosa said, "You see? One good evening can transform a nervous man into a real writer."

Daniel shook his head and smiled. "It didn't transform me," he said. "It only showed me that I was a writer already."

Questions:
What is Daniel's novel about?
It is about a fishing family on the coast of Maine.
What is first book syndrome, according to Rosa?
It is the fear that nobody will come and that people will hate the book.
What were Daniel's and Rosa's predictions?
Daniel predicted five people, and Rosa predicted at least 40.
What did Daniel pledge the night before the launch?
He pledged that he would confront his fear instead of running from it.
Why did Daniel begin with an apology?
He began with an apology because he arrived ten minutes late.
What happened to the books on the table?
They all disappeared, because Mrs. Alvarez sold every copy.

lessons.title: The Bookmobile
lessons.summary: Carla drives the county bookmobile on its weekly route to farms, where a boy borrows a book about fishing.
lessons.text:
Every Wednesday at seven in the morning, Carla Diaz walks around the county bookmobile with a list in her hand. The bookmobile is a large white van full of books, and before each departure, Carla makes a careful inspection. She checks the tires, the lights and the brakes. She also checks the inside, because a heavy box that falls during the trip could hurt someone. Carla never skips the inspection.

The books travel in plastic containers that are tied to the walls with rope. Each container holds about fifty books, and each one has a label: children, cooking, history, farming, novels. Carla ties every rope well and then pulls on it twice, just in case. Last winter, on a road covered with ice, a container slid across the floor.

The departure is at eight sharp. The first hour is on the highway, but after that the roads turn narrow and rough. The van bumps over holes and stones, and the books in the containers bump against each other with a soft sound. Carla drives slowly.

The route has six designated stops: two farms, a country store, a church, a small school and a gas station. At each designated stop, Carla parks the van and opens the side door for her readers.

At the second farm, Mrs. Hanson is waiting by the gate with a sack of returned books. She keeps them in an old flour sack, because it is easy to carry from the house. Carla empties the sack onto the counter, and Mrs. Hanson fills it again with three new novels for the week.

Her son Ben, who is eight, wants a book about fishing. He is holding a fishing rod that is taller than he is. "I want to catch a really big one," he says. Carla finds him a book with pictures of river fish, and Ben promises to read it before he takes his rod to the river on Saturday.

While they talk, a hawk circles slowly over the field. Ben points at it. "That hawk lives in our big tree," he says with pride. Carla looks in another container and finds a book about birds, so Ben takes that one too. Now he can learn about fish and hawks in the same week.

By four in the afternoon, the van is lighter, and the containers are full of returned books. Carla drives home on the same rough roads, tired but happy.

Questions:
What does Carla do before each departure?
She makes a careful inspection of the tires, the lights, the brakes and the inside of the van.
How are the containers held in place?
They are tied to the walls with rope.
Why does the van bump on the way?
After the highway, the roads are narrow and rough, with holes and stones.
How many designated stops does the route have?
The route has six designated stops.
Why does Mrs. Hanson keep her books in a flour sack?
She keeps them in a sack because it is easy to carry from the house.
Which two books does Ben take?
He takes a book about fishing and a book about birds.

lessons.title: The Elephant in the Parade
lessons.summary: Lucy draws a new part of her magazine story about a small elephant, while her son watches and learns.
lessons.text:
Lucy Park draws pictures for children's books and magazines. Her studio is a small room at the top of her house, with a large window, a wooden table and hundreds of pens in old jars. Every surface is covered with paper, and most of that paper is covered with elephants.

For two years, Lucy has been drawing a serial for a children's magazine. Each month, the magazine prints a new part of the serial, and each part tells one of the exploits of Pepper, a small gray elephant who lives in a quiet town. In one month's story, Pepper helped a baker carry bread; in another, she rescued a cat from a tall tree. Children write letters to the magazine to ask about her next exploits.

This month, Pepper will march in the town parade. Lucy begins, as always, with a sketch. She makes a quick sketch of the street, then a sketch of the crowd, then a dozen small sketches of Pepper herself. The hardest part is the proportion. If the ears are too big, Pepper looks silly; if her trunk is too short, she does not look like an elephant at all. To get the proportions right, Lucy studies photos of real elephants, and she keeps an old toy elephant on her table. It is a soft gray doll that she has had since she was six. The doll has lost one eye, but its proportions are perfect.

In the parade picture, a small green bird rides on Pepper's back. The bird used to live in a cage in a shop window, until Pepper set it free. Now the empty cage hangs in Pepper's kitchen, full of flowers.

At four o'clock, Lucy's son Max, who is eleven, comes home from school. Usually he sits in front of the TV with his game controller in his hands. Today, however, he puts the controller down on the couch and comes up to the studio to watch his mother work. "Did you always draw?" he asks.

"Always," Lucy says. "When I was your age, I drew cartoons in the corners of my school books. My teachers were not happy about it. One cartoon showed my math teacher as an elephant."

Max laughs. "Maybe that's where Pepper comes from," he says.

Lucy gives him a pen and a clean sheet of paper. By dinner time, Max has drawn his first cartoon: Pepper in the parade, holding a game controller with her long gray trunk.

Questions:
What does Lucy draw for the children's magazine?
She draws a serial about the exploits of Pepper, a small gray elephant.
What will Pepper do this month?
She will march in the town parade.
Why is the proportion the hardest part?
If the ears or the trunk are the wrong size, Pepper does not look right.
How does Lucy get the proportions right?
She studies photos of real elephants and looks at an old toy elephant doll.
What happened to the bird's cage?
The empty cage now hangs in Pepper's kitchen, full of flowers.
What does Max draw at the end?
He draws a cartoon of Pepper in the parade, holding a game controller.

lessons.title: Please Don't Spoil the Ending
lessons.summary: A slow reader asks friends, family and the internet not to tell her how her novel ends.
lessons.text:
I am a slow reader. A long novel takes me a month, sometimes two. So I have a simple request for everyone: please don't spoil the ending.

At the moment, I am reading a thick novel about a young reporter in a small city. She discovers that the mayor is corrupt: he has been taking money from a building company in exchange for city contracts. The reporter decides to expose him, even though her own editor is afraid. I am on page 300 of 600. I do not know whether she will manage to expose the corrupt mayor, and I do not want to know yet.

Last week, a colleague nearly spoiled it for me. We were standing by the coffee machine when she said, "Oh, that book! Wait until you get to the scandal at the..." I put my hands over my ears like a child, and she stopped. Others are not so kind. Because the novel is about to become a film, there are rumors about the ending all over the internet. I try not to read them, but rumors are hard to avoid, and every day someone online writes about the scandal in the last chapters.

The film will open in the cinema next month. I already know what will happen. The moment it opens, the internet will explode with comments, and every second message will contain the ending. Mainstream films are the worst for this, because everyone sees them in the same week. Last year the same thing happened with a big mainstream film about an earthquake. I had read the book, so I knew how the earthquake scene ended, but my brother had not. When a friend described the ending at dinner, I thought my brother would explode.

My friends and I disagree about all this. My friend Paul says that a good story cannot be spoiled. "If the ending is the only reason you are reading," he says, "it is not a very good book." I disagree. Even a great story loses something when you know what is coming.

So here is my proposal. Provided that a book is less than a year old, or a film is still in the cinema, let us keep the ending to ourselves. Unless someone asks, say nothing. It costs nothing.

As for me, I will finish my novel in about three weeks. Until then, I will not go near the cinema.

Questions:
Why does the writer ask people not to spoil the ending?
She is a slow reader, and she wants to discover the ending herself.
What does the reporter in the novel discover?
She discovers that the mayor is corrupt and takes money from a building company.
Why are there so many rumors about the ending?
There are rumors because the novel is about to become a film.
What will happen when the film opens in the cinema?
The internet will explode with comments, and many messages will contain the ending.
What do the writer and Paul disagree about?
Paul thinks a good story cannot be spoiled, but the writer thinks it always loses something.
What is the writer's proposal?
Unless someone asks, people should not tell the ending of a new book or film.

lessons.title: Keep Our Library Open
lessons.summary: A reader writes to the newspaper to argue against shorter hours at the city library.
lessons.text:
Dear Editor,

I am writing about the city council's plan to reduce the hours of the Central Library in the next fiscal year. Under the plan, the library would close on Sundays and at five o'clock every evening. I understand that the city must balance its budget. Nevertheless, I believe that this plan would be a serious mistake.

Supporters of the plan say that the library has become a liability: an old building that costs money and brings nothing back. I could not disagree more. Last year, more than 200,000 people visited the library. They borrowed books, used the computers, took classes and looked for jobs. A building that serves so many people is not a liability. It is one of the best investments the city makes.

The library matters most to those who have the least. Every morning, homeless men and women wait outside its doors. Inside, they can read the newspaper, charge a phone, write a job application or simply sit somewhere warm and safe. For homeless residents, the evening hours are especially important, because the city shelters do not open until eight. If the library closes at five, where will they go?

The library is also a place of equality. Inside it, a banker and a student, a grandmother and a refugee all have exactly the same rights. Nobody asks who you are or how much money you earn. This kind of equality is rare, and we should protect it. Last month, the library presented a display on the history of racism in our country, and hundreds of families came to see it and talk about it. Honest conversations about racism and equality need public places like this one.

Some will reply that the city treasury is nearly empty. The numbers, however, tell a different story. This spring, the city deployed new parking machines on every downtown street at a considerable cost, and it deployed a team of workers to paint the bridges over the river. Parking machines and fresh paint may be useful. Nevertheless, if the treasury can pay for them, it can also pay for a few hours of library time.

The council will vote on the fiscal plan on Tuesday, March 12, at seven in the evening. I hope that every reader who cares about the library will come and speak.

Best regards,
Martha Quinn

Questions:
What does the city council plan to do?
It plans to reduce the library's hours in the next fiscal year.
Why does Martha think the library is not a liability?
More than 200,000 people visited it last year, so she sees it as one of the city's best investments.
Why are the evening hours important for homeless residents?
They are important because the city shelters do not open until eight.
Why does Martha call the library a place of equality?
Inside the library, everyone has the same rights, and nobody asks how much money you earn.
What did the city deploy this spring?
It deployed new parking machines downtown and a team of workers to paint the bridges.
When will the council vote on the plan?
It will vote on Tuesday, March 12, at seven in the evening.

lessons.title: Grandfather's Book of Carols
lessons.summary: The narrator's grandfather brings his old book of carols and explains two old words while the family sings.
lessons.text:
Every December, my grandfather comes to stay with us for two weeks, and every year he brings the same thing in his bag: a small brown book of carols. It belonged to his mother, and it is virtually falling apart. The cover is held on with tape, and some pages are so thin that you can virtually see through them.

On the first Saturday evening, Grandfather opens the book, and we sing. My mother plays the piano, my little brother Sam sings too loudly, and my father, who claims he cannot sing, pretends to read the newspaper.

This year, Sam stopped in the middle of a carol and asked, "Grandfather, what does 'divine' mean?"

Grandfather took off his glasses. "Divine means 'coming from God,' or 'holy,'" he said. "In the old carols, divine is a big word for something much greater than us. Today some people also call a very good cake divine, but that is not what the carol means."

A few lines later, Sam found the word mercy. Grandfather thought for a moment. "Mercy is kindness that someone does not have to give you," he said. "Imagine that you break my favorite cup. I could be angry with you, but I forgive you instead. That is mercy."

Sam looked at the cup of tea on the piano and moved it carefully away from the edge. Grandfather laughed and slapped his knee, which is what he always does when something makes him laugh. Then he slapped Sam gently on the back. "Don't worry," he said. "I have plenty of mercy left."

"These old carols are full of words like that," he went on. "Divine, mercy, glory, joy. We hardly use them anymore, but they are worth knowing."

Meanwhile, my father had stopped pretending to read. Grandfather looked at him over his glasses and held out the book. For a moment, Dad shook his head. Then he raised both hands in surrender. "All right, I surrender," he said. "One carol." He sang four, and he sang them well.

At the end of the evening, Grandfather closed the book and put it in my hands. "Next year, you can be the one who holds it," he said. I promised to be careful, because a book that is virtually falling apart needs gentle hands.

Questions:
What does Grandfather bring every December?
He brings a small brown book of carols that belonged to his mother.
What does the father do while the family sings?
He pretends to read the newspaper.
What does the word divine mean, according to Grandfather?
It means "coming from God" or "holy."
How does Grandfather explain mercy?
He says that mercy is kindness that someone does not have to give you.
What does Grandfather do when something makes him laugh?
He slaps his knee.
How does the father show that he will sing?
He raises both hands in surrender and says, "All right, I surrender."
